title: Deep well construction without a steep depth penalty

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a repeatable way to construct usable deep wells without a steep increase in the time and cost required for each additional interval of depth. Its target is the whole construction process: reaching the intended formation along a controlled trajectory, installing casing and cement or an equivalent barrier, and demonstrating well integrity. Faster rock removal would contribute to this capability, but would not establish it by itself. These requirements define the proposed concept rather than an established completion standard.

The underlying problem is that deep construction can become much slower and more difficult as temperature, pressure and equipment loads increase. Mechanical drilling nevertheless already reaches extreme depths. CGTN's February 2025 account describes the 10,910 m Shenditake-1 scientific exploration well and more than 300 Tarim Oilfield wells exceeding 8,000 m. Shenditake-1 illustrates a severe late-depth time penalty; it does not establish that contact drilling universally fails in hard rock or beyond a particular depth.

The research identifies non-contact energy, including a proposed millimeter-wave beam that spalls or melts rock, as one possible route. The supplied review could not assess that mechanism because the MIT source had no retained text. The concept therefore remains open to different construction methods: its defining advance is favorable depth scaling for a usable well, rather than adoption of a particular energy source.

significance.text: The revolutionary consequence would be a substantial expansion of practical subsurface access. A repeatable method whose total construction time and cost remain approximately proportional to depth could reduce the economic penalty for reaching deep, difficult formations. The importance of that target is grounded in documented construction constraints: EIA identifies well depth, reservoir pressure and temperature among offshore drilling cost drivers, while Shenditake-1 provides a concrete example of an exceptionally slow final interval. These observations do not establish one universal cost-versus-depth law.

Conditional synthesis: cheaper deep access could make very deep developments or denser well networks more attractive in petroleum production, geothermal energy and scientific drilling. Near-linear scaling alone would not make those choices economical: a method could scale favorably while remaining expensive at every depth. Absolute construction costs, formation productivity, geology, infrastructure and the rest of the development would still determine practical value.

Conditional synthesis: removing an access constraint could enable other reservoir technologies to be deployed more widely, but it would not establish their performance. More affordable wells do not themselves predict multiphase flow, improve reservoir sweep, drain oil from nanopores, convert hydrocarbons underground or bound induced earthquakes. The advance would change where and how economically those capabilities could be attempted.

Conceptual distinction: ordinary improvements in rotary-drilling efficiency and higher-pressure production equipment address related engineering problems. They demonstrate this concept only if they also establish favorable depth scaling for complete well construction. A faster routine shale-well operation or a pressure-rated subsea tree on a conventionally drilled well would not, by itself, show that result.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is integrated construction performance: maintaining useful progress with depth while also delivering the trajectory, barriers and integrity required of a usable well. EIA's cost treatment includes components such as casing and liners, underscoring why rock-removal speed alone is an incomplete measure. Its retained report also cautions against estimating total cost from a single relationship. The reviewed PDF extraction ends during page 52, so it does not provide a complete basis for describing every construction cost or failure mode.

Engineering synthesis: a candidate method must integrate directional control, borehole stability, removal or management of excavated material, pressure control, barrier installation and integrity testing under its intended thermal and mechanical conditions. Improvements at the cutting face could be overwhelmed by slower supporting operations, equipment replacement or remediation. These are proposed engineering questions for assessing the concept; the supplied evidence does not establish that one mechanism dominates all deep-well delays.

Engineering synthesis: for the proposed millimeter-wave route, concrete questions include delivering energy effectively to a deep working face, controlling the resulting borehole geometry, managing spalled or molten material, and integrating the process with steering and well barriers. Performance would need to persist as depth and operating conditions change. The retained material does not establish the technical readiness, failure limits or demonstrated solutions for these questions.

A separate measurement challenge is distinguishing a genuine reduction in the depth penalty from differences in geology, trajectory, well design or market conditions. Shenditake-1's reported timing demonstrates a severe difficulty in one well, but does not isolate depth as the sole cause. EIA's historical cost reductions likewise reflect both efficiency and service-market conditions. A convincing comparison must account for these influences rather than attribute every difference to drilling technology.

current_state.text: CGTN reported on February 20, 2025 that CNPC had completed drilling the 10,910 m Shenditake-1 scientific exploration well in the Tarim Basin. Its operator-attributed account states that reaching 10,000 m took 279 days and the final 910 m required 300 days. Those figures correct the earlier approximations of 270 days and more than 300 days. The report describes oil-and-gas-rich rocks between 10,851 and 10,910 m; that wording does not directly document a hydrocarbon show, commercial flow or a producing completed petroleum well. This is a news account of a pronounced late-depth time penalty, rather than a peer-reviewed time study or controlled experiment isolating depth.

EIA's March 23, 2016 report states that average drilling-and-completion costs in five evaluated U.S. onshore areas in 2015 were 25–30% below their 2012 level. The report attributes savings to improved efficiency and changes in service-market conditions, so the entire reduction cannot be credited to drilling technology. This demonstrates substantial historical cost improvement in existing operations, but does not establish the proposed depth-scaling capability. The review had a complete summary webpage and a partially extracted commissioned report, with the PDF text truncated during page 52.

The research attributes to an MIT Energy Initiative article a Quaise Energy field hole of 118 m in Texas granite in July 2025 and a September 2025 demonstration advancing at up to 5 m per hour. It also attributes to the company's vice president of engineering a comparison with commercial mechanical granite drilling averaging about 0.1 m per hour. These are unverified reports within the supplied research: no article text was retained for the review, so the dimensions, dates, rates and comparability could not be checked. Even if confirmed, a peak advance rate and a company-supplied average benchmark would not by themselves establish total construction speed or cost.

The same research describes the Quaise hole as neither a cased, directionally controlled petroleum well nor a test at geothermal temperature. Those configuration and temperature claims also remain unverified because the MIT text is unavailable. The supplied material cannot determine whether later company remarks about greater depth described an independently reported completed well. In addition, the research dates the MIT article November 3, 2025; that bibliographic date could not be checked against retained article content.

For the related pressure-equipment comparison, the research attributes to Chevron an August 2024 production start at Anchor, equipment rated to 20,000 psi, reservoir depths of approximately 30,000–34,000 ft below sea level, and a maximum reservoir temperature of 250 °F (121 °C). It describes 15,000 psi as the preceding subsea limit. Neither Chevron source had retained content available to the review, so these specifications and the production date cannot serve here as verified historical benchmarks. Regardless of their eventual verification, equipment pressure ratings and complete-well depth scaling remain distinct capabilities.

The supplied bibliography names a 2014 study, Cost analysis of oil, gas, and geothermal well drilling, as a source for a depth-resolved well-cost index. However, the retained DOI response contained only a redirect message, without identifiable article content. Its methods and conclusions therefore cannot be used here to establish a cost formula or universal depth penalty.

Evidence boundary: the supplied freshness search record is empty, so these historical reports do not establish the latest state as of November 1, 2026. The reviewed material does not demonstrate achievement of the integrated capability proposed here. That limitation also does not establish that no qualifying demonstration has occurred elsewhere or since the dated reports.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration, not an established standard: construct more than one directional well to a specified reservoir depth in hard or hot rock, install casing and cement or an explicitly justified equivalent barrier, and pass defined integrity tests. Specify trajectory tolerances, borehole dimensions, operating temperature and pressure, and intended well use before testing. A shallow open-hole rock-removal test would demonstrate only part of this capability.
completion_criteria.label: Multiple directional wells reach reservoir depth and pass integrity tests

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scaling test: measure cumulative construction days and total construction cost against depth across a preselected interval where comparable mechanical offset wells exhibit a steepening penalty. Define the acceptable departure from linearity and absolute cost and time targets in advance. Include supporting operations, barrier installation, equipment interventions and remediation in the accounting, with clear start and end points. Match or transparently adjust comparisons for geology, trajectory, dimensions, barrier design and market conditions.
completion_criteria.label: Full construction time and cost meet predefined depth-scaling targets

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirement: retain auditable depth-resolved operating records, costs, integrity results and failures, and obtain independent assessment of the comparison. Repeat successful construction sufficiently to establish performance beyond a single favorable well. Demonstrations spanning different rock types, temperatures or depths would establish broader applicability, but any finite program would demonstrate performance within tested conditions rather than literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Repeated construction performance is independently assessed using auditable records

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: state the depth, temperature, pressure, geology and trajectory range within which the method has been demonstrated, together with equipment life, intervention requirements and sustained progress. A favorable scaling curve should be accompanied by absolute economics and usable-well performance. Production-equipment ratings alone would not satisfy these construction criteria, and a successful construction demonstration would not itself prove reservoir productivity or project profitability.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrated operating limits, absolute economics and usable-well performance are reported

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — PET-01, Blind prediction of multiphase reservoir flow: cheaper deep wells could provide access for measurements and prospective tests of reservoir predictions. PET-07 concerns construction performance; PET-01 concerns predicting how multiple fluid phases move after access is available.

Roster-based synthesis — PET-02, Conventional-oil recovery at gas-field recovery factors: more affordable wells could expand options for reservoir contact and development. High recovery still requires effective displacement and sweep; construction economics alone do not establish the proposed recovery factor.

Roster-based synthesis — PET-03, Commercial gas production from methane hydrate: improved well access could assist some hydrate developments, but commercial hydrate production has separate production and reservoir-management requirements. PET-07's deep-well target should not be assumed necessary or sufficient for every hydrate setting.

Roster-based synthesis — PET-04, Industrial in-situ conversion of oil-shale kerogen: lower construction costs could support layouts requiring multiple subsurface wells. The conversion process, product recovery and industrial operating performance remain separate breakthroughs.

Roster-based synthesis — PET-05, Shale-oil recovery from the matrix: better well access could improve the economics of contacting a formation, while recovery from the matrix depends on mobilizing and transporting oil through very small pores. Additional or cheaper wells do not by themselves solve that transport problem.

Roster-based synthesis — PET-06, Hydrogen from petroleum reservoirs, with the other products left underground: PET-07 could reduce the access cost for injection, production or monitoring. It does not establish underground hydrogen generation, selective recovery or retention of the other products.

Roster-based synthesis — PET-08, Permeability and saturation measured through the reservoir volume: cheaper wells could enable additional observation locations and access for instruments. PET-08's defining advance is measurement across the reservoir volume; constructing more wells does not establish that coverage or accuracy.

Roster-based synthesis — PET-09, Bitumen that flows at native reservoir temperature: favorable construction economics could reduce development costs, but would not establish bitumen mobility under native conditions. The access problem and the fluid-mobility problem remain distinct.

Roster-based synthesis — PET-10, A pressure plan with a prospectively tested earthquake bound: affordable wells could broaden pressure-management and monitoring options. Demonstrating a prospective earthquake bound requires separate predictive evidence; successful deep construction does not supply that bound.

Roster-based synthesis — PET-11, In-reservoir conversion of bitumen to pipeline-specification crude: improved access could support a conversion development, but the underground conversion, product quality and recovery requirements belong to PET-11. PET-07 establishes neither conversion chemistry nor pipeline compliance.

change_log.reason: The useful distinction is between integrated construction and isolated rock removal, rather than between particular drilling mechanisms.

change_log.reason: The supplied evidence also documents successful mechanical drilling at extreme depths and does not establish universal failure conditions.

unresolved_issues: The MIT article's content and bibliographic date remain unverified. Its reported mechanism, 118 m demonstration, July and September 2025 dates, rates, configuration and temperature require inspectable evidence.
The basis and comparability of the company-attributed 0.1 m per hour mechanical granite benchmark are unknown; peak rock-removal speed cannot establish a complete-well economic advantage.
The supplied material cannot determine whether later Quaise depth remarks represented independently documented, barrier-equipped and integrity-tested wells.

Anchor's reported production date, 20,000 psi rating, preceding 15,000 psi limit, reservoir depths and temperature remain unverified in the retained material. The review's recommendation to remove these specifications entirely was not adopted: they are preserved only as explicitly unverified research claims, to retain useful context without treating them as evidence.

The research's historical target above 30,000 psi and 500 °F lacks verified support and is not retained as a factual benchmark. Whether a further equipment rating would open a separate resource class also remains unresolved.
The cited 2014 cost study's scientific content is unavailable in the retained DOI response, and the commissioned EIA report extraction is incomplete.
The Shenditake-1 timing account does not isolate the contributions of depth, geology, equipment, operational decisions and other delays.
Acceptable near-linearity, absolute economic targets, required depth range, offset comparability and sufficient replication remain choices to define before a demonstration.
The empty freshness record prevents a conclusion about the latest demonstrated capability as of November 1, 2026.

brief.title: Deep wells without sharply rising construction costs
possible: People could reach deep underground formations without each extra stretch taking much longer and costing much more to build. The result would be usable wells with controlled paths and tested barriers against leaks.
why: Cheaper deep access could make more sites practical for oil and gas production, energy from underground heat, and scientific drilling. It could also make denser networks of wells more attractive.

sources.showed: This is a report of a field demonstration using a millimeter-wave beam, a form of electromagnetic energy, to break or melt rock.
sources.cited_for: It describes a possible route to faster rock removal.
sources.not_established: Rock removal alone does not establish the time or cost of constructing a usable deep well.

sources.who: U.S. Energy Information Administration and IHS Global Inc.
sources.showed: Their cost study found that improved operations and changes in service markets reduced well construction costs.
sources.quote: This evolution resulted in reduced drilling and completion times, lower total well costs, and increased well performance.
sources.cited_for: Well costs can fall through better engineering and changing market conditions.
sources.not_established: Historical savings do not establish that construction costs can remain roughly proportional to depth.

sources.who: Authors of “Cost analysis of oil, gas, and geothermal well drilling”
sources.showed: This is a study of well-drilling costs described as a source for a cost index organised by depth.
sources.cited_for: It concerns the relationship between drilling costs and depth.
sources.not_established: A cost index alone would not demonstrate a method that avoids sharply rising construction costs.

sources.showed: CNPC completed drilling the exceptionally deep Shenditake-1 scientific well. Its reported final stretch took longer than all the drilling before it.
sources.quote: To support the project, CNPC developed the world's first 12,000-meter automated drilling rig and a suite of advanced ultra-deep well logging tools.
sources.cited_for: Mechanical drilling reaches extreme depths, but progress can slow severely near the bottom.
sources.not_established: This single well does not isolate depth from geology, equipment problems or other causes of delay.

sources.showed: This is an announcement of production starting at Anchor using equipment designed for high pressures.
sources.cited_for: It describes related progress in equipment for deep offshore production.
sources.not_established: Equipment pressure ratings do not demonstrate how total well construction time and cost change with depth.

sources.showed: This is a fact sheet describing Anchor's reservoir conditions and production equipment.
sources.cited_for: It provides context on the conditions that deep production equipment must withstand.
sources.not_established: Operating production equipment under pressure does not establish cheaper construction of deeper wells.

shown: CNPC drilled Shenditake-1 to 10,910 metres using mechanical drilling. Its account describes severe slowing near the bottom. Existing operations have also achieved substantial cost savings, but neither result demonstrates repeatable construction without a steep depth penalty.
missing: A method still needs to combine deep drilling, steering, stable hole walls, debris management, pressure control and tested barriers.
Full construction measurements must show that supporting work and repairs do not erase gains in rock-removal speed.
Repeated wells must establish the advantage against comparable conventional wells, with independent assessment.

milestones.label: Multiple deep wells follow planned paths and pass leak tests
milestones.explanation: Multiple wells would have to reach a specified depth in hard or hot rock, follow planned paths and pass tests of their protective barriers. This would establish usable construction.

milestones.label: Total time and cost meet agreed targets across depths
milestones.explanation: Full construction time and cost would have to meet predefined targets as depth increases, against comparable conventional wells. This would establish whether the depth penalty has fallen.

milestones.label: Independent assessment confirms repeatable construction performance
milestones.explanation: Repeated construction would have to withstand independent assessment using auditable operating, cost, failure and barrier-test records. This would establish performance beyond a favourable well.

milestones.label: Operating limits, actual costs and usable wells are demonstrated
milestones.explanation: Results would have to state tested operating conditions, equipment life, repair needs, actual costs and usable-well performance. This would define where the method has practical value.

uncertain: How close to proportional must time and cost remain as depth increases, and over what depth range?
How many repeated wells would establish reliability, and how should differences in geology, design and market conditions be accounted for?
Could favourable growth in costs with depth still leave wells too expensive to justify?

page.title: Deep-well construction with linear depth scaling
page.definition: A method constructs wells whose total construction time and cost grow no faster than linearly with true vertical depth, the vertical distance below the surface. Delivered wells follow their specified trajectories and pass the well-barrier tests required for their intended use.

goal.need: Across five U.S. onshore oil-and-gas areas, average drilling-and-completion costs in 2015 were 25–30% below 2012 levels; EIA attributes the reduction to operational efficiency and service-market conditions. DOE reports that casing and cement can account for as much as 50% of geothermal well-construction costs. Reducing rock-removal time therefore addresses only part of the construction cost.

figures.caption: Reported drilling times for the Shenditake-1 scientific exploration well
figures.note: One well; CNPC account reported by CGTN on 20 February 2025, updated on 22 February 2025. The comparison does not isolate depth from geology and operational difficulties.

statements.body: U.S. Department of Energy, Geothermal Technologies Office
statements.quote: Improve drilling costs toward the “ideal” cost curves used in the GeoVision analysis

statements.body: U.S. Department of Energy, Geothermal Drilling Technology Demonstration Campaign
statements.quote: The ultimate goal of this FOA is a reduction in geothermal well costs.
statements.context: The funding announcement specifies a 25% improvement in average daily drilling penetration rate as its performance target.

statements.quote: The cost model indicates that MMW drilling could reach twice that depth at drilling costs of around $1,000 per meter.
statements.context: The antecedent depth is 10 km. MMW means millimeter-wave drilling; the passage describes a model presented at the World Geothermal Congress.

completion.title: Repeated deep-well construction shows no increase in time or cost per additional metre of depth.
completion.criterion: Repeated construction of wells at different true vertical depths demonstrates that incremental total construction time and cost per additional metre do not increase across a prospectively specified deep interval. Wells have comparable geology, trajectories, diameters and operating conditions. Accounting includes construction through verified well integrity, including steering, barriers, interruptions and remediation. Each well meets its applicable trajectory and barrier acceptance requirements. Achievement applies only within the demonstrated depth and operating envelope.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; proposed operational definition without an externally established numerical acceptance threshold.
completion.basis: Searches of DOE GeoVision and its implementation plan, DOE drilling-demonstration requirements, API material and developer publications found no integrated time-and-cost-versus-depth acceptance test, including a depth range, statistical tolerance or replication count. DOE specifies drilling-rate improvement; Quaise reports modelled cost per metre. The proposed test retains complete construction and repeated performance.

milestones.title: A well-construction method validates a critical function in laboratory experiments.
milestones.criterion: Analytical and laboratory studies validate a critical function of the proposed well-construction process, meeting technology readiness level 3. A 2023 Stanford Geothermal Workshop abstract reports full-bore vaporization of hard crystalline rock using millimeter waves. The abstract supplies neither specimen count nor bore dimensions.
milestones.set_by: DOE EERE, R 540.112-02, TRL 3; generic process criterion. DOE also uses readiness levels in its geothermal drilling programme.
milestones.threshold_quote: Proof of concept validation has been achieved

milestones.title: A pilot well-construction system demonstrates engineering feasibility under representative conditions.
milestones.criterion: A pilot demonstrates engineering feasibility in actual or high-fidelity conditions relevant to its intended wells, meeting technology readiness level 6. On 3 November 2025, MIT Energy Initiative reported that Quaise drilled one 118 m field hole in July 2025. This institutional news report is not peer reviewed and does not document qualification of an integrated well-construction system.
milestones.set_by: DOE EERE, R 540.112-02, TRL 6; generic process criterion.

milestones.title: A well-construction prototype operates near full scale in its intended operating environment.
milestones.criterion: A near-full-scale prototype operates with ancillary systems in the environment of its intended wells, meeting technology readiness level 7. On 7 July 2026, Quaise reported that its Central Texas drilling system was approaching 1 km depth. That company press release, which is not peer reviewed, supplies no completed kilometre-depth result or integrated construction qualification.
milestones.set_by: DOE EERE, R 540.112-02, TRL 7; generic process criterion.
milestones.threshold_quote: System prototyping demonstration in operational environment.

milestones.title: A complete well-construction system meets its end-user specifications in full-scale testing.
milestones.criterion: The full-scale construction system operates with its hardware and software integrated; testing demonstrates its end-user specifications, meeting technology readiness level 8. Applied to this capability, qualification covers the complete construction process and delivered well. The cited Quaise field reports do not document this result. Repeated demonstration of the required depth scaling remains the completion test.
milestones.set_by: DOE EERE, R 540.112-02, TRL 8; generic process criterion, without a drilling-cost threshold.

not_found: No well-specific published qualification sequence was found for complete construction with linear time and cost scaling; the milestones use DOE's generic maturity criteria.
The cited field reports provide no repeated, depth-resolved measurements combining complete-well construction time, cost and integrity.
The supplied 2014 drilling-cost paper could not be opened through either its DOI or publisher page.
Both supplied Chevron sources returned access errors.
The full 2014 MIT rock-exposure report and its DOE final-report counterpart could not be opened.

results.finding: One full-scale scientific exploration well was drilled to 10,910 meters.
results.detail: The report describes deep drilling and liner cementing, but does not establish complete well-construction qualification, trajectory and barrier acceptance, or the required depth scaling.
results.quote: The China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) announced on Thursday that it has completed the drilling of the deepest vertical well in Asia, with a borehole reaching a depth of 10,910 meters in China's northwestern desert.

results.finding: RePED electro-crushing drilled one granite sample to a depth of 9 inches.
results.detail: The project also modeled well costs and tested critical drilling components. The report does not establish linear depth scaling or demonstrate a complete downhole system.
results.quote:
To address the 
second barrier to commercialization, a 9” hole was drilled through a sample block of granite, 
demonstrating the tool’s effectiveness in hard rock.

results.finding: In one test well, dual downhole drive units drilled 66 ft of hard rock.
results.detail: The field test used the drive subsystem on conventional drill pipe in a real crystalline-rock well. The full coiled-tubing system had not been integrated, and the source does not establish qualification of a complete well-construction system at TRL 6.
results.quote: A total of 66 ft (approximately 20 m) of hard Phyllite was drilled over 7.5 continuous hours of operation.

results.finding: RePED drilled 1 hole 9 inches deep in a granite sample.
results.detail: The hard-rock demonstration supports drilling feasibility, but it did not qualify an integrated well-construction system under representative well conditions. High-temperature components still needed downhole validation.
results.quote: To address the second barrier to commercialization, a 9” hole was drilled through a sample block of granite, demonstrating the tool’s effectiveness in hard rock.

results.finding: Two downhole drive units drilled 20 m of hard phyllite in a Norwegian test well.
results.detail: The integrated units operated in a full-scale test facility, but they were a subsystem tested on conventional drill pipe. Integration with the full coiled-tubing system and extended-duration validation remained future work.
results.quote: A total of 66 ft (approximately 20 m) of hard Phyllite was drilled over 7.5 continuous hours of operation.

results.finding: Quaise millimeter-wave drilling produced a 100-inch-deep hole in 2023; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The company describes laboratory development and a 1-inch-diameter hole, but does not report the analytical studies needed to establish the criterion as written.
results.quote: In 2023, we hit our 100x target of a 1” diameter hole at 100” deep.

results.finding: In 15 Barre Granite comminution tests, inferred quartz removal rates were at least 10 times the predicted dissolution rate.
results.detail: Analysis and laboratory tests demonstrated rock removal under simulated deep-well conditions. Pure-water tests did not establish continuous spallation or recover rock spalls; chemically enhanced tests produced holes and recovered spalls, but penetrated only part of each sample.
results.quote:
The difference in the observed comminution rate from the quartz 
dissolution rate implies that a secondary mechanism preferentially removing quartz exists.

results.finding: Plasma-pulse drilling in granite, sample size unstated: productivity fell to about 60% of baseline at 40 MPa.
results.detail: Laboratory experiments and modeling address rock fracture, a critical drilling function. The source does not establish that the method achieves linear depth scaling or identify its work as the specified 2023 Stanford abstract.
results.quote: Increasing the lithostatic pressure up to 40 MPa reduces PPGD performance (i.e., productivity decreases to around 60% and Specific energy increases by 75% from their baseline values), which is unfavorable for the PPGD process.
